How unbelievable it is that God can take a wretched sinner, void of the fear of the Lord, and turn him into a blood-washed saint and preacher of the gospel! In this story, we see God’s life-changing power at work in our hymn writer’s life.

In the small cemetery of a churchyard in Olney, England, stands a granite tombstone with this inscription, written by Newton himself before his death:

John Newton, once an infidel and libertine, a servant of slaves in Africa, was, by the rich mercy of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, preserved, restored, pardoned, and appointed to preach the faith he had long labored to destroy!

This epitaph aptly describes the unusual and colorful life of this man, one of the great evangelical preachers of the eighteenth century. His testimony was, “By the grace of God, I am what I am!”

“Amazing Grace” was a hymn published in 1779, with words written in 1772 by the English poet and Anglican clergyman John Newton (1725–1807). “Amazing Grace” is probably the most beloved hymn of the last two centuries. This hymn is estimated to be performed 10 million times annually. It has appeared on over 11,000 albums and translated into about 60 languages. It was referenced in Harriet Beecher Stowe’s anti-slavery novel Uncle Tom’s Cabin. It had a surge in popularity during two of America’s greatest crises: the Civil War and the Vietnam War.

Ironically, this stirring song, closely associated with the African-American community, was written by a former slave trader, John Newton.

John was born on July 24, 1725, in Wapping, England, to a seafaring father, John Newton, Sr., and a devout Christian mother, Elizabeth Newton. His father loved him but was gone at sea most of the time. On the other hand, his mother was tender and nurturing, teaching him the Word of God. She would instruct him in memorizing the Bible whole chapters at a time and took him to church. Unfortunately, when he was almost seven, his mother died of tuberculosis. His father remarried a short time later and sent him to a boarding school. During his time at the boarding school, he made bad friends. His character disintegrated to the point that he was dismissed from one school and moved to another. By the time he was 11 years old, the boarding schools didn’t want him, so his father took him along to sea. He spent the next six years on the Atlantic Ocean with his father.

When John was 17, his father arranged to send him to Jamaica for a well-paying job overseeing a plantation. On his way, while waiting for the ship’s departure, John received an invitation to the home of some old-time friends, the Catletts. It was in this home that John’s mother had died ten years earlier. As he reacquainted himself with them, he got to know their daughter, Mary. John and Mary’s mothers were best of friends. John had been invited to stay four days, but he stayed two weeks and missed the ship to Jamaica.

At age 18, John was conscripted into the Royal Navy, and his life went from bad to worse. He wanted to return and see Mary, so he deserted the ship but was caught, publicly flogged, and laid in irons. His life on the ship was so profane that even the other ungodly sailors cringed at his curses and blasphemies. He gained the title “The Great Blasphemer” and was such an unwanted man on the ship that he was sent to work on a slave ship.

One of the owners of the slave ship where he now worked, offered John a job once they reached the African coast. However, once on shore, he was tied up and forced to work with little food, clothing, or shelter. He sent several letters back to his father during this time, pleading for help.

A ship called The Greyhound was sailing near the coast, which John had now called home. The captain had been instructed by John’s father to look for his son. The ship, while being almost too far from shore to trade, decided to give trading a try. A friend of John’s rowed out from shore to trade. As he turned to leave, the captain asked him whether he knew anyone named John Newton. He did to the captain’s surprise, and John was brought on board to go home.

On board the ship, Newton picked up a copy of Thomas á Kempis’s Christian classic, The Imitation of Christ. He had never encountered anything like it, and he began to wonder if the Christian claims might be true. That night, on March 10, 1748, a fierce storm nearly swamped the ship. Men, animals, and provisions were swept overboard. The storm awakened Newton, the ship’s rotten timbers broken by the waves and floodwater swirling into his cabin. John prayed for the first time in years.

The Greyhound thrashed about in the North Atlantic storm for over 11 days. With little hope of survival, the sailors mechanically worked the pumps, trying to keep the vessel afloat. On the eleventh day of the storm, John was too exhausted to pump, so he was tied to the helm, where he did his best to hold the ship to its course. From one o’clock until midnight, he was at the helm. He feared he was going to die, and if the Christian faith were true, then he surely would not be forgiven. He reflected on all he had done over the past few years. His life seemed as ruined and wrecked as the battered ship he was trying to steer through the storm. During those long and grueling hours, Newton cried out to God like he never had before, and that was the turning point in his life.

That was a day John Newton remembered ever after. “On that day, the Lord sent from on high and delivered me out of deep waters.” Over 50 years later, John wrote in his diary on March 21, 1805: “Not well able to write; but I endeavor to observe the return of this day with humiliation, prayer, and praise.”

Only God’s amazing grace could take a rude, profane, slave-trading sailor and transform him into a child of God. John never ceased to stand in awe of God’s work in his life. He took an interest in prayer, reading and meditating on the Scriptures, and only speaking words pleasing to God.

On his return home, Mary and her parents recognized the change the Lord had brought in John. The two were married on February 1, 1750.

For the next four years, Newton was captain of his own slave ship. This occupation kept him separated from Mary for months at a time. While they were apart, the two corresponded constantly. In his letters, John repeatedly wrote how their love and marriage increased his thankfulness and gratefulness to the Lord. “... When I indulge myself with a particular thought of you, it usually carries me on farther and brings me upon my knees to bless the Lord for giving me such a treasure and to pray for your peace and welfare”

John endeavored to “Christianize” his slave ship by holding Sunday services for his crew of 30 sin-hardened men. He made three more voyages to bring slaves from Africa to North America. As he planned his fourth trip, he became sick with malaria. God used this sickness to end his involvement in the slave trade.

As John began a new chapter in his life, he felt called to be a minister. For more than 50 years, he preached the gospel and was one of the most influential men of his day.

John Newton often composed a hymn to go with his Sunday evening services. In 1779, 280 of these were collected and combined with 68 hymns by Newton’s friend and parishioner, William Cowper, and published as the Olney Hymns. The most famous of all the Olney Hymns, “Faith’s Review and Expectation”, grew out of David’s exclamation in 1 Chronicles 17:16-17. We know it today as “Amazing Grace”. “Amazing Grace” originally had six stanzas, and the last verse was added about a century later. Most hymnals have four or five of these verses.

As minister in the church, John continued to be more and more troubled by the slave trade that was still going on. In 1788, 34 years after he left the slave trade, He wrote a book entitled Thoughts Upon the African Slave Trade and sent it to all the members of parliament. This book brought an awareness to the public of the evils of the slave trade. He quotes this, “Needless to say, the capturing, selling and transporting of black slaves to the plantations in the West Indies and America was a cruel and vicious way of life.” With the help and providence of God, John saw the day, several months before his death, in 1807, when slavery was officially banned from England.

When John was in his sixties, his beloved wife Mary passed away. This was a great trial for John, and he spent the remaining 17 years of his life without her.

After John suffered a stroke and shortly before his death, a spokesman for the church encouraged Newton to consider retiring from preaching because of failing health, eyesight, and memory. John replied, “What, shall the old African blasphemer stop while he can still speak? I will continue to preach. Although my memory’s fading, I remember two things very clearly: I am a great sinner, and Christ is a great Savior.”

The last words of John Newton as he lay on his deathbed were as follows: “I am still in the land of the dying; I shall be in the land of the living soon.”

The tune “Amazing Grace” is an early American folk melody. It was first known as a plantation melody entitled “Loving Lambs”. This tune was first published in 1831 in the book The Virginia Harmony. The majority of hymn books published after this time included this song. In 1910, Edwin O. Excell added the last verse, which eventually replaced the last three original verses of the song. His edition of the song is most common in our hymnals today. Several other Olney hymns by Newton continue to be sung today, including “How Sweet the Name of Jesus Sounds” and “Glorious Things of Thee are Spoken”.

Hvor utrolig det er at Gud kan ta en elendig synder, uten gudsfrykt, og gjøre ham om til en blodvasket hellig mann og forkynner av evangeliet! I denne fortellingen ser vi Guds livsforvandlende kraft virke i vår salmepresters liv.

I den lille kirkegården ved en kirke i Olney, England, står en gravstein i granitt med denne innskriften, skrevet av Newton selv før hans død:

John Newton, engang en vantro og utsvevende mann, en tjener for slaver i Afrika, ble, ved vår Herre og Frelser Jesus Kristus’ rike miskunn, bevart, gjenopprettet, tilgitt og satt til å forkynne den tro han lenge hadde anstrengt seg for å ødelegge!

Denne epitafen beskriver treffende den uvanlige og fargerike tilværelsen til denne mannen, en av de store evangeliske forkynnerne på 1700-tallet. Hans vitnesbyrd var: «Ved Guds nåde er jeg hva jeg er!»

“Amazing Grace” var en salme utgitt i 1779, med tekst skrevet i 1772 av den engelske dikteren og anglikanske presten John Newton (1725–1807). «Amazing Grace» er sannsynligvis den mest elskede salmen de siste to århundrene. Det anslås at denne salmen fremføres 10 millioner ganger årlig. Den har dukket opp på over 11 000 album og blitt oversatt til rundt 60 språk. Den ble referert til i Harriet Beecher Stowes antislaveroman Uncle Tom’s Cabin. Den fikk et oppsving i popularitet under to av Amerikas største kriser: borgerkrigen og Vietnamkrigen.

Ironisk nok ble denne gripende sangen, som ofte forbindes med det afro-amerikanske miljøet, skrevet av en tidligere slavehandler, John Newton.

John ble født 24. juli 1725 i Wapping, England, av en sjøfarende far, John Newton Sr., og en from kristen mor, Elizabeth Newton. Far elsket ham, men var mesteparten av tiden til sjøs. Hans mor derimot var øm og oppdragende, og hun lærte ham Guds ord. Hun holdt ham til å memorere hele bibelkapitler og tok ham med i kirken. Dessverre døde hans mor av tuberkulose da han var nesten syv år. Faren giftet seg på nytt kort tid etter og sendte ham på kostskole. I løpet av tiden på kostskolen fikk han dårlige venner. Hans karakter raknet til det punkt at han ble kastet ut av en skole og sendt til en annen. Da han var 11 år, ville ikke kostskolene ha ham lenger, så far tok ham med til sjøs. Han tilbrakte de neste seks årene på Atlanterhavet sammen med faren.

Når John var 17, ordnet faren en godt betalt stilling for ham på Jamaica hvor han skulle overse en plantasje. På vei dit, mens han ventet på skipets avgang, mottok John en invitasjon til hjemmet til noen gamle venner, familien Catlett. Det var i dette hjemmet Johns mor hadde dødd ti år tidligere. Mens han gjenopptok bekjentskapet med dem, ble han kjent med deres datter, Mary. Johns og Marys mødre hadde vært bestevenner. John hadde blitt invitert til å bli fire dager, men han ble to uker og gikk glipp av skipet til Jamaica.

Da han var 18, ble John innrullert i Royal Navy, og livet hans gikk fra vondt til verre. Han ønsket å vende tilbake for å se Mary, så han deserterte, men ble tatt, offentlig pisket og lagt i lenker. Livet om bord var så gudløst at selv de andre ugudelige sjøfolkene rygget ved hans banning og bespottelser. Han fikk tilnavnet «Den store blasfemiker» og var så uønsket om bord at han ble sendt for å arbeide på et slaveskip.

En av eierne av slaveskipet hvor han nå arbeidet, tilbød John en stilling når de nådde Afrikas kyst. Men da han kom i land, ble han bundet og tvunget til å arbeide med lite mat, klær eller husly. Han sendte flere brev hjem til faren i denne perioden og ba om hjelp.

Et skip kalt The Greyhound seilte nær kysten, som John nå hadde kalt hjem. Kapteinen hadde fått instruksjoner fra Johns far om å lete etter sønnen. Skipet, selv om det var nesten for langt fra kysten til å drive handel, besluttet å prøve. En venn av John rodde ut fra kysten for å handle. Da han snudde for å dra, spurte kapteinen om han kjente noen ved navn John Newton. Til kapteinens overraskelse gjorde han det, og John ble brakt om bord for å reise hjem.

Ombord plukket Newton opp en kopi av Thomas á Kempis’ kristne klassiker, The Imitation of Christ. Han hadde aldri møtt noe lignende, og begynte å undre seg på om de kristne påstandene kunne være sanne. Den natten, 10. mars 1748, var det et voldsomt uvær som nesten kantret skipet. Menn, dyr og proviant ble feid over bord. Stormen vekket Newton; skipets råtne spant ble brutt av bølgene, og flomvannet virvlet inn i hans lugar. John ba for første gang på mange år.

The Greyhound raste rundt i Nord-Atlanterens uvær i over 11 dager. Med liten håp om å overleve arbeidet sjøfolkene mekanisk med pumpene for å holde fartøyet flytende. På den ellevte dagen var John for utmattet til å pumpe, så han ble bundet til rattet, hvor han gjorde sitt beste for å holde skipet på kurs. Fra ett til midnatt var han ved roret. Han fryktet at han skulle dø, og hvis den kristne tro var sann, ville han sikkert ikke bli tilgitt. Han reflekterte over alt han hadde gjort de siste årene. Hans liv virket like ødelagt og forlist som det herjede skipet han forsøkte å styre gjennom stormen. I de lange og utmattende timene ropte Newton til Gud som han aldri hadde gjort før, og det ble vendepunktet i hans liv.

Det var en dag John Newton husket resten av livet. «På den dagen sendte Herren fra det høye og frelste meg ut av dype vann.» Mer enn 50 år senere skrev John i sin dagbok 21. mars 1805: «Ikke godt i stand til å skrive; men jeg forsøker å markere denne dagens tilbakekomst med ydmykelse, bønn og lovprisning.»

Bare Guds fantastiske nåde kunne ta en grov, frekk, slavehandlende sjømann og forvandle ham til Guds barn. John sluttet aldri å stå i ærefrykt for Guds verk i hans liv. Han interesserte seg for bønn, lesning og meditasjon over Skriftene, og prøvde bare å tale ord som behaget Gud.

På hjemreisen gjenkjente Mary og hennes foreldre forandringen Herren hadde brakt over John. De to ble viet 1. februar 1750.

De neste fire årene var Newton kaptein på sitt eget slaveskip. Dette yrket holdt ham adskilt fra Mary i måneder om gangen. Mens de var fra hverandre, korresponderte de stadig. I brevene skrev John gjentatte ganger hvordan deres kjærlighet og ekteskap økte hans takknemlighet og takksigelser til Herren. «... Når jeg tillater meg å tenke spesielt på deg, fører det meg som regel videre og bringer meg på kne for å velsigne Herren for å ha gitt meg en slik skatt og for å be for din fred og velferd»

John forsøkte å «kristne» slaveskipet sitt ved å holde søndagsgudstjenester for besetningen på 30 hardbarkede menn. Han foretok tre flere reiser for å hente slaver fra Afrika til Nord-Amerika. Mens han forberedte sin fjerde reise, ble han syk av malaria. Gud brukte denne sykdommen til å få ham ut av slavehandelen.

Da John begynte et nytt kapittel i livet, følte han seg kalt til å bli prest. I mer enn 50 år forkynte han evangeliet og var en av sin tids mest innflytelsesrike menn.

John Newton komponerte ofte en salme til søndagskveldsgudstjenestene sine. I 1779 ble 280 av disse samlet og kombinert med 68 salmer av Newtons venn og menighetsmedlem William Cowper, og utgitt som Olney Hymns. Den mest berømte av alle Olney-hymnene, «Faith’s Review and Expectation», vokste fram av Davids utrop i 1 Chronicles 17:16-17. Vi kjenner den i dag som «Amazing Grace». «Amazing Grace» hadde opprinnelig seks vers, og det siste verset ble lagt til omtrent et århundre senere. De fleste salmebøker har fire eller fem av disse versene.

Som prest i kirken ble John mer og mer opptatt av slavehandelen som fortsatt pågikk. I 1788, 34 år etter at han forlot slavehandelen, skrev han en bok med tittelen Thoughts Upon the African Slave Trade og sendte den til alle parlamentsmedlemmer. Denne boken skapte offentlig bevissthet om ondskapene ved slavehandelen. Han skriver dette: «Selvsagt var fangst, salg og transport av svarte slaver til plantasjene i Vestindia og Amerika en grusom og ond måte å leve på.» Med Guds hjelp og forsyn så John dagen, noen måneder før sin død i 1807, da slaveri offisielt ble forbudt i England.

Da John var i sekstiårene, døde hans elskede kone Mary. Dette ble en stor prøve for John, og han tilbrakte de resterende 17 årene av sitt liv uten henne.

Etter at John led et slag og kort tid før sin død, oppfordret en talsmann for kirken Newton til å vurdere å gå av som forkynner på grunn av sviktende helse, syn og hukommelse. John svarte: «Hva, skal den gamle afrikanske blasfemiker stoppe mens han ennå kan tale? Jeg vil fortsette å forkynne. Selv om hukommelsen svinner, husker jeg to ting svært klart: Jeg er en stor synder, og Kristus er en stor Frelser.»

John Newtons siste ord på dødsleiet var som følger: «Jeg er fortsatt i de døendes land; jeg skal snart være i de levendes land.»

Melodien til «Amazing Grace» er en tidlig amerikansk folkemelodi. Den var først kjent som en plantagemelodi med tittelen «Loving Lambs». Denne melodien ble først utgitt i 1831 i boka The Virginia Harmony. Flertallet av salmebøkene utgitt etter dette tidspunktet inkluderte denne sangen. I 1910 la Edwin O. Excell til det siste verset, som etter hvert erstattet de tre siste opprinnelige versene i sangen. Hans utgave av sangen er den mest vanlige i våre salmebøker i dag. Flere andre Olney-salmer av Newton synges fortsatt i dag, inkludert «How Sweet the Name of Jesus Sounds» og «Glorious Things of Thee are Spoken».

How unbelievable it is that God can take a wretched sinner, void of the fear of the Lord, and turn him into a blood-washed saint and preacher of the gospel! In this story, we see God’s life-changing power at work in our hymn writer’s life.

In the small cemetery of a churchyard in Olney, England, stands a granite tombstone with this inscription, written by Newton himself before his death:

John Newton, once an infidel and libertine, a servant of slaves in Africa, was, by the rich mercy of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, preserved, restored, pardoned, and appointed to preach the faith he had long labored to destroy!

This epitaph aptly describes the unusual and colorful life of this man, one of the great evangelical preachers of the eighteenth century. His testimony was, “By the grace of God, I am what I am!”

“Amazing Grace” was a hymn published in 1779, with words written in 1772 by the English poet and Anglican clergyman John Newton (1725–1807). “Amazing Grace” is probably the most beloved hymn of the last two centuries. This hymn is estimated to be performed 10 million times annually. It has appeared on over 11,000 albums and translated into about 60 languages. It was referenced in Harriet Beecher Stowe’s anti-slavery novel Uncle Tom’s Cabin. It had a surge in popularity during two of America’s greatest crises: the Civil War and the Vietnam War.

Ironically, this stirring song, closely associated with the African-American community, was written by a former slave trader, John Newton.

John was born on July 24, 1725, in Wapping, England, to a seafaring father, John Newton, Sr., and a devout Christian mother, Elizabeth Newton. His father loved him but was gone at sea most of the time. On the other hand, his mother was tender and nurturing, teaching him the Word of God. She would instruct him in memorizing the Bible whole chapters at a time and took him to church. Unfortunately, when he was almost seven, his mother died of tuberculosis. His father remarried a short time later and sent him to a boarding school. During his time at the boarding school, he made bad friends. His character disintegrated to the point that he was dismissed from one school and moved to another. By the time he was 11 years old, the boarding schools didn’t want him, so his father took him along to sea. He spent the next six years on the Atlantic Ocean with his father.

When John was 17, his father arranged to send him to Jamaica for a well-paying job overseeing a plantation. On his way, while waiting for the ship’s departure, John received an invitation to the home of some old-time friends, the Catletts. It was in this home that John’s mother had died ten years earlier. As he reacquainted himself with them, he got to know their daughter, Mary. John and Mary’s mothers were best of friends. John had been invited to stay four days, but he stayed two weeks and missed the ship to Jamaica.

At age 18, John was conscripted into the Royal Navy, and his life went from bad to worse. He wanted to return and see Mary, so he deserted the ship but was caught, publicly flogged, and laid in irons. His life on the ship was so profane that even the other ungodly sailors cringed at his curses and blasphemies. He gained the title “The Great Blasphemer” and was such an unwanted man on the ship that he was sent to work on a slave ship.

One of the owners of the slave ship where he now worked, offered John a job once they reached the African coast. However, once on shore, he was tied up and forced to work with little food, clothing, or shelter. He sent several letters back to his father during this time, pleading for help.

A ship called The Greyhound was sailing near the coast, which John had now called home. The captain had been instructed by John’s father to look for his son. The ship, while being almost too far from shore to trade, decided to give trading a try. A friend of John’s rowed out from shore to trade. As he turned to leave, the captain asked him whether he knew anyone named John Newton. He did to the captain’s surprise, and John was brought on board to go home.

On board the ship, Newton picked up a copy of Thomas á Kempis’s Christian classic, The Imitation of Christ. He had never encountered anything like it, and he began to wonder if the Christian claims might be true. That night, on March 10, 1748, a fierce storm nearly swamped the ship. Men, animals, and provisions were swept overboard. The storm awakened Newton, the ship’s rotten timbers broken by the waves and floodwater swirling into his cabin. John prayed for the first time in years.

The Greyhound thrashed about in the North Atlantic storm for over 11 days. With little hope of survival, the sailors mechanically worked the pumps, trying to keep the vessel afloat. On the eleventh day of the storm, John was too exhausted to pump, so he was tied to the helm, where he did his best to hold the ship to its course. From one o’clock until midnight, he was at the helm. He feared he was going to die, and if the Christian faith were true, then he surely would not be forgiven. He reflected on all he had done over the past few years. His life seemed as ruined and wrecked as the battered ship he was trying to steer through the storm. During those long and grueling hours, Newton cried out to God like he never had before, and that was the turning point in his life.

That was a day John Newton remembered ever after. “On that day, the Lord sent from on high and delivered me out of deep waters.” Over 50 years later, John wrote in his diary on March 21, 1805: “Not well able to write; but I endeavor to observe the return of this day with humiliation, prayer, and praise.”

Only God’s amazing grace could take a rude, profane, slave-trading sailor and transform him into a child of God. John never ceased to stand in awe of God’s work in his life. He took an interest in prayer, reading and meditating on the Scriptures, and only speaking words pleasing to God.

On his return home, Mary and her parents recognized the change the Lord had brought in John. The two were married on February 1, 1750.

For the next four years, Newton was captain of his own slave ship. This occupation kept him separated from Mary for months at a time. While they were apart, the two corresponded constantly. In his letters, John repeatedly wrote how their love and marriage increased his thankfulness and gratefulness to the Lord. “... When I indulge myself with a particular thought of you, it usually carries me on farther and brings me upon my knees to bless the Lord for giving me such a treasure and to pray for your peace and welfare”

John endeavored to “Christianize” his slave ship by holding Sunday services for his crew of 30 sin-hardened men. He made three more voyages to bring slaves from Africa to North America. As he planned his fourth trip, he became sick with malaria. God used this sickness to end his involvement in the slave trade.

As John began a new chapter in his life, he felt called to be a minister. For more than 50 years, he preached the gospel and was one of the most influential men of his day.

John Newton often composed a hymn to go with his Sunday evening services. In 1779, 280 of these were collected and combined with 68 hymns by Newton’s friend and parishioner, William Cowper, and published as the Olney Hymns. The most famous of all the Olney Hymns, “Faith’s Review and Expectation”, grew out of David’s exclamation in 1 Chronicles 17:16-17. We know it today as “Amazing Grace”. “Amazing Grace” originally had six stanzas, and the last verse was added about a century later. Most hymnals have four or five of these verses.

This book brought an awareness to the public of the evils of the slave trade. He quotes this, “Needless to say, the capturing, selling and transporting of black slaves to the plantations in the West Indies and America was a cruel and vicious way of life.” With the help and providence of God, John saw the day, several months before his death, in 1807, when slavery was officially banned from England.

When John was in his sixties, his beloved wife Mary passed away. This was a great trial for John, and he spent the remaining 17 years of his life without her.

After John suffered a stroke and shortly before his death, a spokesman for the church encouraged Newton to consider retiring from preaching because of failing health, eyesight, and memory. John replied, “What, shall the old African blasphemer stop while he can still speak? I will continue to preach. Although my memory’s fading, I remember two things very clearly: I am a great sinner, and Christ is a great Savior.”

The last words of John Newton as he lay on his deathbed were as follows: “I am still in the land of the dying; I shall be in the land of the living soon.”

His edition of the song is most common in our hymnals today. Как невероятно, что Бог может взять жалкого грешника, лишённого страха пред Господом, и превратить его в омытого кровью святого и проповедника Евангелия! В этой истории мы видим действенную, изменяющую жизнь силу Божью в жизни нашего автора гимна.

На невысоком кладбище при приходской церкви в Олни, Англия, стоит гранитный надгробный камень со следующей надписью, написанной самим Ньюлтоном перед смертью:

Джон Ньютон, когда‑то неверующий и распутник, слуга работорговцев в Африке, был по богатой милости нашего Господа и Спасителя Иисуса Христа сохранён, восстановлен, прощён и назначен проповедовать веру, которую он долгие годы старался уничтожить!

Это эпитафия удачно описывает необычную и красочную жизнь этого человека, одного из великих евангельских проповедников XVIII века. Его свидетельство было таким: «По благодати Божией я то, что я есть!»

«Удивительная благодать» — гимн, опубликованный в 1779 году, со словами, написанными в 1772 году английским поэтом и англиканским священником Джоном Ньютоном (1725–1807). «Удивительная благодать» вероятно самый любимый гимн последних двух столетий. По оценкам, этот гимн исполняется 10 миллионов раз в год. Он попал на более чем 11 000 альбомов и переведён примерно на 60 языков. На него ссылалась Гарриет Бичер-Стоу в её антирабовладельческом романе «Хижина дяди Тома». Популярность гимна возросла в двух из величайших американских кризисов: во время Гражданской войны и войны во Вьетнаме.

Иронично, что эта трогательная песня, тесно связанная с афро‑американским сообществом, была написана бывшим работорговцем, Джоном Ньютоном.

Джон родился 24 июля 1725 года в Уоппинге, Англия, в семье морского капитана Джона Ньютона-старшего и набожной матери Элизабет Ньютон. Отец любил его, но большую часть времени находился в море. Зато мать была нежной и заботливой, учила его Божьему Слову. Она поучала его, помогая заучивать целые главы Библии, и водила его в церковь. К несчастью, когда ему было почти семь лет, мать умерла от туберкулёза. Отец вскоре женился во второй раз и отправил его в пансион. Во время учёбы в пансионе у него появились плохие друзья. Его характер деградировал до такой степени, что его исключили из одной школы и перевели в другую. К одиннадцати годам пансионы уже не принимали его, и отец взял сына с собой в море. Следующие шесть лет он провёл в Атлантическом океане с отцом.

Когда Джону было 17, отец устроил ему выгодную должность надзирателя на плантации в Ямайке. По пути, ожидая отплытия корабля, Джон получил приглашение в дом старых друзей — семьи Катлеттов. Именно в этом доме десять лет назад умерла мать Джона. При воссоединении с ними он познакомился с их дочерью Мэри. Мать Джона и мать Мэри были лучшими подругами. Джона приглашали остаться на четыре дня, но он задержался на две недели и пропустил корабль на Ямайку.

В восемнадцать лет Джона призвали на королевский флот, и его жизнь пошла только хуже. Он хотел вернуться к Мэри, поэтому дезертировал, но был пойман, публично порот и закован в железа. Его поведение на корабле было настолько богохульным, что даже другие безбожные моряки отвращались от его ругательств и богохульств. Он получил прозвище «Великий богохульник» и был настолько нежелан на корабле, что его отправили работать на работорговое судно.

Один из владельцев работоргового судна, на котором он теперь служил, предложил Джону работу, когда они достигнут африканского побережья. Однако, оказавшись на берегу, его связали и принудили работать при скудном питании, почти без одежды и укрытия. В это время он отправил несколько писем отцу с мольбой о помощи.

Вблизи берега ходил корабль «The Greyhound», который Джон теперь называл своим домом. Капитану было дано указание от отца Джона искать его сына. Корабль, едва находясь в пределах досягаемости для торговли, всё же решил попытать счастье. Друг Джона отвёз лодкой торговцев от берега. Когда он отплывал, капитан спросил его, знает ли он кого‑нибудь по имени Джон Ньютон. К удивлению капитана тот ответил утвердительно, и Джона пригласили на борт, чтобы он вернулся домой.

На борту корабля Ньютон взял в руки копию христианской классики Томаса а Кемписа «Подражание Христу». Он никогда прежде не сталкивался с чем‑то подобным, и начал задумываться, неужели христианские утверждения могут быть истинны. В ту ночь, 10 марта 1748 года, свирепый шторм едва не потопил корабль. Люди, животные и провиант были смыты за борт. Шторм разбудил Ньютона: гнилые балки судна ломались волнами, и в его каюту хлынула вода. Джон в первый раз за многие годы помолился.

The Greyhound больше 11 дней барахтался в североатлантическом шторме. Почти без надежды на спасение моряки механически работали помпами, пытаясь удержать судно на плаву. На одиннадцатый день шторма Джон был настолько изнурён, что не мог качать помпу, поэтому его привязали к штурвалу, где он изо всех сил старался держать курс. С одного часа до полуночи он стоял у руля. Он боялся, что умрёт, и если христианская вера истинна, то ему уж точно не будет прощено. Он размышлял обо всём, что натворил за последние годы. Его жизнь казалась такой же разрушенной и разбитой, как и повреждённое судно, которое он пытался провести через бурю. В те долгие и изнурительные часы Ньютон взывал к Богу, как никогда прежде, и это стало поворотным моментом в его жизни.

Это был день, который Джон Ньютон помнил всю оставшуюся жизнь. «В тот день Господь послал сверху и избавил меня из глубокой воды». Более чем через 50 лет Джон записал в своём дневнике 21 марта 1805 года: «Не в силах хорошо писать; но я стараюсь соблюдать возвращение этого дня с покаянием, молитвой и хвалою».

Только удивительная благодать Божья могла взять грубого, богохульного моряка‑работорговца и превратить его в ребёнка Божьего. Джон никогда не переставал благоговеть перед делом Бога в своей жизни. Он стал уделять внимание молитве, чтению и размышлению над Писанием и старался говорить лишь слова, угодные Богу.

По возвращении домой Мэри и её родители увидели перемену, которую Господь совершил в Джоне. Они поженились 1 февраля 1750 года.

Следующие четыре года Ньютон был капитаном собственного работоргового судна. Эта должность разлучала его с Мэри на месяцы. Во время разлук они постоянно переписывались. В письмах Джон неоднократно писал, как их любовь и брак увеличивают его благодарность Господу. «…Когда я позволяю себе особенную мысль о вас, она обычно уносит меня дальше и ставит на колени, чтобы благословить Господа за то, что дал мне такое сокровище, и молиться за ваш мир и благополучие».

Джон стремился «очеловечить» своё работорговое судно, проводя воскресные богослужения для команды из 30 закалённых в грехе людей. Он совершил ещё три плавания за рабами из Африки в Северную Америку. Планируя четвёртое путешествие, он заболел малярией. Бог использовал эту болезнь, чтобы положить конец его участию в работорговле.

Начав новую главу своей жизни, он почувствовал призвание к служению священника. Более 50 лет он проповедовал Евангелие и стал одним из самых влиятельных людей своего времени.

Джон Ньютон часто сочинял гимн к своим воскресным вечерним службам. В 1779 году 280 таких гимнов были собраны и объединены с 68 гимнами друга и прихожанина Ньютона, Уильяма Коупера, и изданы под названием Olney Hymns. Самым известным из всех Olney Hymns, «Обзор веры и ожидание» (Faith’s Review and Expectation), появившимся из восклицания Давида в 1 Паралипоменон 17:16–17, мы знаем сегодня как «Удивительная благодать». Первоначально «Удивительная благодать» имела шесть строф; последняя строфа была добавлена примерно через столетие. В большинстве гимнарей встречаются четыре или пять из этих строф.

Будучи служителем церкви, Ньютон всё больше и больше мучился из‑за продолжающейся работорговли. В 1788 году, через 34 года после того, как он покинул работорговлю, он написал книгу под названием Thoughts Upon the African Slave Trade и разослал её всем членам парламента. Эта книга привлекла внимание общественности к злу работорговли. Он писал: «Разумеется, захват, продажа и перевозка чёрных рабов на плантации в Вест‑Индии и Америке была жестоким и порочным образом жизни». С помощью и провидением Божьим Джон увидел тот день, за несколько месяцев до своей смерти в 1807 году, когда рабство официально было запрещено в Англии.

Когда Джону было за шестьдесят, его любимая жена Мэри умерла. Это было большим испытанием для Джона, и он провёл оставшиеся 17 лет своей жизни без неё.

После того как Джон перенёс инсульт и незадолго до смерти, представитель церкви призвал Ньютона подумать о выходе на покой из‑за ухудшающегося здоровья, зрения и памяти. Джон ответил: «Что ж, неужели старый африканский богохульник перестанет, пока ещё может говорить? Я буду продолжать проповедовать. Хотя память моя тускнеет, два вещи я помню очень ясно: я — великий грешник, и Христос — великий Спаситель».

Последние слова Джона Ньютона, лежащего на смертном одре, были такими: «Я всё ещё в земле умирающих; скоро я буду в стране живых».

Мелодия «Удивительной благодати» — ранняя американская народная мелодия. Первоначально она была известна как плантационная мелодия под названием «Loving Lambs». Эта мелодия была впервые опубликована в 1831 году в книге The Virginia Harmony. Большинство гимнарей, издававшихся после этого времени, включали эту песню. В 1910 году Эдвин О. Экскелл добавил последнюю строфу, которая в конце концов заменила последние три оригинальные строфы песни. Его редакция песни наиболее распространена в наших гимнарах сегодня. Несколько других Olney Hymns Ньютона продолжают петься и поныне, включая «How Sweet the Name of Jesus Sounds» и «Glorious Things of Thee are Spoken».

How unbelievable it is that God can take a wretched sinner, void of the fear of the Lord, and turn him into a blood-washed saint and preacher of the gospel! In this story, we see God’s life-changing power at work in our hymn writer’s life.

In the small cemetery of a churchyard in Olney, England, stands a granite tombstone with this inscription, written by Newton himself before his death:

John Newton, once an infidel and libertine, a servant of slaves in Africa, was, by the rich mercy of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, preserved, restored, pardoned, and appointed to preach the faith he had long labored to destroy!

This epitaph aptly describes the unusual and colorful life of this man, one of the great evangelical preachers of the eighteenth century. His testimony was, “By the grace of God, I am what I am!”

“Amazing Grace” was a hymn published in 1779, with words written in 1772 by the English poet and Anglican clergyman John Newton (1725–1807). “Amazing Grace” is probably the most beloved hymn of the last two centuries. This hymn is estimated to be performed 10 million times annually. It has appeared on over 11,000 albums and translated into about 60 languages. It was referenced in Harriet Beecher Stowe’s anti-slavery novel Uncle Tom’s Cabin. It had a surge in popularity during two of America’s greatest crises: the Civil War and the Vietnam War.

Ironically, this stirring song, closely associated with the African-American community, was written by a former slave trader, John Newton.

John was born on July 24, 1725, in Wapping, England, to a seafaring father, John Newton, Sr., and a devout Christian mother, Elizabeth Newton. His father loved him but was gone at sea most of the time. On the other hand, his mother was tender and nurturing, teaching him the Word of God. She would instruct him in memorizing the Bible whole chapters at a time and took him to church. Unfortunately, when he was almost seven, his mother died of tuberculosis. His father remarried a short time later and sent him to a boarding school. During his time at the boarding school, he made bad friends. His character disintegrated to the point that he was dismissed from one school and moved to another. By the time he was 11 years old, the boarding schools didn’t want him, so his father took him along to sea. He spent the next six years on the Atlantic Ocean with his father.

When John was 17, his father arranged to send him to Jamaica for a well-paying job overseeing a plantation. On his way, while waiting for the ship’s departure, John received an invitation to the home of some old-time friends, the Catletts. It was in this home that John’s mother had died ten years earlier. As he reacquainted himself with them, he got to know their daughter, Mary. John and Mary’s mothers were best of friends. John had been invited to stay four days, but he stayed two weeks and missed the ship to Jamaica.

At age 18, John was conscripted into the Royal Navy, and his life went from bad to worse. He wanted to return and see Mary, so he deserted the ship but was caught, publicly flogged, and laid in irons. His life on the ship was so profane that even the other ungodly sailors cringed at his curses and blasphemies. He gained the title “The Great Blasphemer” and was such an unwanted man on the ship that he was sent to work on a slave ship.

One of the owners of the slave ship where he now worked, offered John a job once they reached the African coast. However, once on shore, he was tied up and forced to work with little food, clothing, or shelter. He sent several letters back to his father during this time, pleading for help.

A ship called The Greyhound was sailing near the coast, which John had now called home. The captain had been instructed by John’s father to look for his son. The ship, while being almost too far from shore to trade, decided to give trading a try. A friend of John’s rowed out from shore to trade. As he turned to leave, the captain asked him whether he knew anyone named John Newton. He did to the captain’s surprise, and John was brought on board to go home.

On board the ship, Newton picked up a copy of Thomas á Kempis’s Christian classic, The Imitation of Christ. He had never encountered anything like it, and he began to wonder if the Christian claims might be true. That night, on March 10, 1748, a fierce storm nearly swamped the ship. Men, animals, and provisions were swept overboard. The storm awakened Newton, the ship’s rotten timbers broken by the waves and floodwater swirling into his cabin. John prayed for the first time in years.

The Greyhound thrashed about in the North Atlantic storm for over 11 days. With little hope of survival, the sailors mechanically worked the pumps, trying to keep the vessel afloat. On the eleventh day of the storm, John was too exhausted to pump, so he was tied to the helm, where he did his best to hold the ship to its course. From one o’clock until midnight, he was at the helm. He feared he was going to die, and if the Christian faith were true, then he surely would not be forgiven. He reflected on all he had done over the past few years. His life seemed as ruined and wrecked as the battered ship he was trying to steer through the storm. During those long and grueling hours, Newton cried out to God like he never had before, and that was the turning point in his life.

That was a day John Newton remembered ever after. “On that day, the Lord sent from on high and delivered me out of deep waters.” Over 50 years later, John wrote in his diary on March 21, 1805: “Not well able to write; but I endeavor to observe the return of this day with humiliation, prayer, and praise.”

Only God’s amazing grace could take a rude, profane, slave-trading sailor and transform him into a child of God. John never ceased to stand in awe of God’s work in his life. He took an interest in prayer, reading and meditating on the Scriptures, and only speaking words pleasing to God.

On his return home, Mary and her parents recognized the change the Lord had brought in John. The two were married on February 1, 1750.

For the next four years, Newton was captain of his own slave ship. This occupation kept him separated from Mary for months at a time. While they were apart, the two corresponded constantly. In his letters, John repeatedly wrote how their love and marriage increased his thankfulness and gratefulness to the Lord. “... When I indulge myself with a particular thought of you, it usually carries me on farther and brings me upon my knees to bless the Lord for giving me such a treasure and to pray for your peace and welfare”

John endeavored to “Christianize” his slave ship by holding Sunday services for his crew of 30 sin-hardened men. He made three more voyages to bring slaves from Africa to North America. As he planned his fourth trip, he became sick with malaria. God used this sickness to end his involvement in the slave trade.

As John began a new chapter in his life, he felt called to be a minister. For more than 50 years, he preached the gospel and was one of the most influential men of his day.

John Newton often composed a hymn to go with his Sunday evening services. In 1779, 280 of these were collected and combined with 68 hymns by Newton’s friend and parishioner, William Cowper, and published as the Olney Hymns. The most famous of all the Olney Hymns, “Faith’s Review and Expectation”, grew out of David’s exclamation in 1 Chronicles 17:16-17. We know it today as “Amazing Grace”. “Amazing Grace” originally had six stanzas, and the last verse was added about a century later. Most hymnals have four or five of these verses.

As minister in the church, John continued to be more and more troubled by the slave trade that was still going on. In 1788, 34 years after he left the slave trade, He wrote a book entitled Thoughts Upon the African Slave Trade and sent it to all the members of parliament. This book brought an awareness to the public of the evils of the slave trade. He quotes this, “Needless to say, the capturing, selling and transporting of black slaves to the plantations in the West Indies and America was a cruel and vicious way of life.” With the help and providence of God, John saw the day, several months before his death, in 1807, when slavery was officially banned from England.

When John was in his sixties, his beloved wife Mary passed away. This was a great trial for John, and he spent the remaining 17 years of his life without her.

After John suffered a stroke and shortly before his death, a spokesman for the church encouraged Newton to consider retiring from preaching because of failing health, eyesight, and memory. John replied, “What, shall the old African blasphemer stop while he can still speak? I will continue to preach. Although my memory’s fading, I remember two things very clearly: I am a great sinner, and Christ is a great Savior.”

The last words of John Newton as he lay on his deathbed were as follows: “I am still in the land of the dying; I shall be in the land of the living soon.”

The tune “Amazing Grace” is an early American folk melody. It was first known as a plantation melody entitled “Loving Lambs”. This tune was first published in 1831 in the book The Virginia Harmony. The majority of hymn books published after this time included this song. In 1910, Edwin O. Excell added the last verse, which eventually replaced the last three original verses of the song. His edition of the song is most common in our hymnals today. Several other Olney hymns by Newton continue to be sung today, including “How Sweet the Name of Jesus Sounds” and “Glorious Things of Thee are Spoken”.

כמה זה לא יאומן שאלוהים יכול לקחת חוטא מושחת, חסר יראת ה', ולהפכו לקדוש שטופף בדמו ונביא הבשורה! בסיפור זה אנו רואים את כוחו המשנה-חיים של אלוהים פועל בחיי מחבר המנון זה.

בבית הקברות הקטן של חצר כנסייה באולניּי, אנגליה, עומדת מצבת גרניט עם הכיתוב הבא, שכתב ניוטון בעצמו לפני מותו:

ג'ון ניוטון, פעם כחול-ראשון וחיל הַמפות, עבד עבדים באפריקה, היה על-ידי רחמי האדירים של אדוננו ומושיענו ישוע המשיח, שמור, מְשׁוּבָּץ, מחול, ומיועד לדרוש את האמונה שבה נאבק זמן רב להחריב!

כתובת קבורה זו מתארת במדויק את חייו המיוחדים והצבעוניים של האיש הזה, אחד מן הווקים הנוצריים המובילים במאה השמונה-עשרה. עדותו הייתה: "בחסד אלוהים, אני מה שאני!"

"Amazing Grace" ("חסד מופלא") היה מנון שפורסם ב-1779, עם מילים שנכתבו ב-1772 על ידי המשורר האנגלי וכומר האנגלקני ג'ון ניוטון (1725–1807). "חסד מופלא" הוא כנראה המנון הנערץ ביותר בשני המאות האחרונות. ההערכה היא שמנון זה מושמע כעשרה מיליון פעמים בשנה. הוא הופיע בלמעלה מ-11,000 אלבומים ותרגום ל־כ-60 שפות. הוא מוזכר ברומן האנטי-עבדות של הארייט בקר סטו, Uncle Tom’s Cabin. הוא חווה גל פופולריות במהלך שניים מן המשברים הגדולים באמריקה: מלחמת האזרחים ומלחמת וייטנאם.

אירוני כי שיר זה המעורר רגשות, המשויך בקירבה לקהילה האפרו-אמריקאית, נכתב על ידי סוחר עבדים לשעבר, ג'ון ניוטון.

ג'ון נולד ב-24 ביולי 1725 בבאפּינג, אנגליה, לאב ימאי, ג'ון ניוטון האב, ואם נוצרית אדוקה, אליזבת ניוטון. אביו אהב אותו אך שהה רוב הזמן בים. מצד שני, אימו הייתה עדינה ומטפחת, לימדה אותו את דבר ה' והנחתה אותו לשנן פרקי תנ"ך שלמים וללקחת אותו לכנסייה. למרבה הצער, כשהיה כמעט בן שבע, אמו מתה מטובורקולוזיס. אביו התחתן בשנית זמן קצר לאחר מכן ושלח אותו לבית ספר לפנימייה. בתקופת שהותו בפנימייה הכיר חברים רעים. אופיו התמוטט עד כדי that פוטר מבית ספר אחד והועבר לאחר. עד גיל 11, בתי-הפנימייה כבר לא רצו אותו, אז אביו לקח אותו עמו לים. הוא בילה את ששת השנים הבאות באוקיינוס האטלנטי עם אביו.

כשהיה ג'ון בן 17, אביו סידר לשלוחו לג'מייקה לעבודה משולמת שבה היה אמור לפקח על מטע. בדרכו, בהמתנה לצאת האונייה, ג'ון קיבל הזמנה לביתם של חברים וותיקי־זמן, משפחת קטלט. זהו אותו בית שבו אמו של ג'ון מתה לפני עשר שנים. כשהתחדש הקשר עימם, הכיר את בתם, מרי. אמהותיהם של ג'ון ומרי היו החברות הטובות ביותר. ג'ון הוזמן להישאר ארבעה ימים, אך נשאר שבועיים ופספס את האונייה לג'מייקה.

בגיל 18 גויס ג'ון לצי המלכותי, וחייו הלכו מגרוע לגרוע. רצה לשוב ולראות את מרי, לכן נמלט מן האונייה אך נתפס, הוכה בציבור והושם בשרשראות. חייו על האונייה היו כה שטניסטים שהימאים החסרי-יראת אף הם גינו את קללותיו ואת כפישתיו. הוא זכה לכינוי "החיל הגדול" והיה אדם בלתי רצוי כל כך על האונייה עד שנשלח לעבוד על ספינת עבדים.

אחד מבעלי ספינת העבדים שבה עבד כעת, הציע לג'ון עבודה כשהם יגיעו לחופי אפריקה. אך כשהגיעו לחוף, הוקשר וחויב לעבוד בתנאים של מזון, לבוש ומקלט דלים. בשעה זו שלח כמה מכתבים חזרה לאביו, מתחנן לעזרה.

ספינה בשם The Greyhound הפליגה ליד החוף, שהפך עתה לביתו של ג'ון. הקפטן קיבל הוראה מאביו של ג'ון לשים עין על בנו. הספינה, אף שהייתה כמעט רחוקה מדי מן החוף למסחר, החליטה לנסות. חבר של ג'ון התרחק בחירה לשם סחר. כשהתהפך להחלוף, הקפטן שאל אותו אם הוא מכיר מישהו בשם ג'ון ניוטון. להפתעת הקפטן ענה בחיוב, וג'ון הובא אל הסיפון כדי לשוב הביתה.

על הסיפון נשא ניוטון עותק מהמונוגרפיה הנוצרית של תומאס אַ קמפיס, The Imitation of Christ. מעולם לא נתקל בדבר דומה, והחל לתהות האם טענות הנצרות עשויות להיות אמת. באותו לילה, ב-10 במרץ 1748, סערה עזה כמעט וטיבעה את הספינה. בני אדם, בעלי-חיים ואספקה נשטפו אל הים. הסערה העיר את ניוטון; קרשי הספינה הרקובים נשברו על ידי הגלים ומי השיטפון גלשו לתאיו. ג'ון התפלל בפעם הראשונה מזה שנים.

The Greyhound סערה וסחפה בסערת הצפון האטלנטית במשך למעלה מ־11 יום. עם תקווה מועטה להינצל, המלחים עבדו את עבודתם באופן מכני, מפעילים את המשאבות בניסיון לשמור על כלי השיט צף. ביום האחד-עשר של הסערה, ג'ון היה מותש מדי מכדי לפעול במשאבות, ולכן הוקשר להגה, שם עשה את מיטב יכולתו לשמור את הספינה על קורסה. מאחת בצהריים ועד חצות הוא ישב בהגה. חשש שהוא עומד למות, ואם האמונה הנוצרית אמתית, הרי שלא יימחל לו. חשב בכל מה שעשה בשנים האחרונות. חייו נראו כי חרבו ונרמסו כשם שהספינה ההרוסה שאותה ניסה לנווט דרך הסערה. בשעות הארוכות והקשות ההן, ניוטון זעק אל אלוהים כמעולם לא זעק, וזאת היתה נקודת המפנה בחייו.

זהו יום שג'ון ניוטון זכר מאז ועד סופו. "ביום ההוא שלח ה' מלמעלה והצילני מתוך מים עמוקים." למעלה מ־50 שנה לאחר מכן כתב ניוטון ביומנו ב-21 במרץ 1805: "לא מסוגל היטב לכתוב; אך אני משתדל לציין את שובו של יום זה בענווה, בתפילה ובשבח."

רק חסד אלוהים המופלא יכל לקחת ימאי גס, שטני וסוחר עבדים ולהפכו לילד של אלוהים. ג'ון לא חדל להימלא יראת כבוד מפעל האלוהים בחייו. הוא נטה להתפלל, לקרוא ולהרהר בכתבי הקודש, ולדבר אך מילים הנעימות לאלוהים.

עם שובו הביתה, מרי והוריה זיהו את השינוי שהביא ה' בג'ון. השניים נישאו ב־1 בפברואר 1750.

בארבע השנים שלאחר מכן שימש ניוטון כקפטן של ספינת עבדים משלו. עיסוק זה החזיק אותו נפרד ממרי חודשים ארוכים בכל פעם. בזמן היעדרם הם החליפו מכתבים ללא הפסקה. במכתביו כתב ג'ון שוב ושוב כיצד אהבתם ונישואיהם הגבירו את תודעתו והכרתו הטובה לאדון. "... כאשר אני מפנק את עצמי במחשבה מיוחדת עלייך, זה בד"כ נושא אותי רחוק יותר ומביאני על ברכי להתברך את ה' על שניתן לי אוצר כזה ולבקש את שלומך וטובתך"

ג'ון ניסה "להנצר" את ספינת העבדים שלו על ידי קיום תפילות יום ראשון עבור צוותו של 30 גברים המתקשים בעוונותיהם. הוא עשה שלושה מסעות נוספים להביא עבדים מאפריקה לצפון אמריקה. כאשר תכנן את מסעו הרביעי, חלה במלריה. אלוהים השתמש במחלה זו כדי לסיים את מעורבותו בסחר בעבדים.

כשהחל פרק חדש בחייו של ג'ון, חש קריאה להיות משרת. במשך יותר מ־50 שנה דרש את הבשורה והיה אחד האנשים המשפיעים ביותר בימיו.

ג'ון ניוטון לעתים קרובות חיבר מנון שישתלב בשירותי הערב של יום ראשון. ב-1779 נאספו 280 מן המנונים הללו וצורפו ל־68 מנונים מאת ידידו ותושב עיירתו, ויליאם קאופר, ופורסמו כ־Olney Hymns. המנון המפורסם מכל ה־Olney Hymns, "Faith’s Review and Expectation", צמח מתוך קריאתו של דויד ב־דברי הימים א' יז:16–17. אנו מכירים אותו היום כ"חסד מופלא". ל"חסד מופלא" בתחילה היו שישה בתים, והבית האחרון נוסף כמאה שנים לאחר מכן. ברוב ספרי המנונים מופיעים ארבעה או חמישה מן הבתים הללו.

כשכומר בכנסייה, נמשך ייסורו של ג'ון דווקא מהמחשבה על סחר העבדים שעדיין נמשך. ב־1788, 34 שנים לאחר שעזב את סחר העבדים, כתב ספר שכותרתו Thoughts Upon the African Slave Trade ושלח אותו לכל חברי הפרלמנט. ספר זה העלה את מודעות הציבור לרעות שבסחר בעבדים. הוא מצטט זאת: "אין צורך לומר, החטיפה, המכירה והובלת עבדים שחורים למטעים בהאיים המערביים ובאמריקה הייתה דרך חיים אכזרית ושחצנית." בעזרת ובשגחה של אלוהים ראה ג'ון את היום, מספר חודשים לפני מותו, ב־1807, שבו העבדות נאסרה רשמית באנגליה.

כשהיה ג'ון בשנות השישים לחייו, אשתו היקרה מרי נפטרה. זו הייתה נסיון קשה עבור ג'ון, והוא בילה את שבע־עשרה השנים האחרונות לחייו בלעדיה.

לאחר שג'ון סבל משבץ ולפני מותו בקצרה, דובר הכנסייה עודד את ניוטון לשקול לפרוש מתורתו מפאת בריאות לקויה, ראייה וזיכרון מתדרדרים. ג'ון השיב: "מה, האם יפסיק הבלע האפריקני הישן בעודו יכול עדיין לדבר? אמשיך לדרוש. אף שהזיכרון שלי דועך, אני זוכר שתי דברים בבירור: אנכי חוטא גדול, ומשיח הוא מושיע גדול."

המילים האחרונות של ג'ון ניוטון כששכב על ערש הדומיה היו כדלקמן: "אני עדיין בארץ המתים; אתקן להיות בקרוב בארץ החיים."

הנושא המוזיקלי של "חסד מופלא" הוא נעימה עממית אמריקנית מוקדמת. הוא הוכר תחילה כנעימת מטע תחת השם "Loving Lambs". נושא זה פורסם לראשונה ב־1831 בספר The Virginia Harmony. רובה של ספרי המנונים שפורסמו לאחר מועד זה הכילו שיר זה. ב־1910 הוסיף אדווין או. אקסל את הבית האחרון, שהחליף לבסוף את שלושת הבתים האחרונים המקוריים של השיר. מהדורתו של השיר היא המקובלת ביותר בספרי המנונים שלנו היום. מספר מנונים נוספים מתוך ה־Olney hymns של ניוטון ממשיכים להישמע עד היום, ביניהם "How Sweet the Name of Jesus Sounds" ו"Glorious Things of Thee are Spoken".

How unbelievable it is that God can take a wretched sinner, void of the fear of the Lord, and turn him into a blood-washed saint and preacher of the gospel! In this story, we see God’s life-changing power at work in our hymn writer’s life.

In the small cemetery of a churchyard in Olney, England, stands a granite tombstone with this inscription, written by Newton himself before his death:

John Newton, once an infidel and libertine, a servant of slaves in Africa, was, by the rich mercy of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, preserved, restored, pardoned, and appointed to preach the faith he had long labored to destroy!

This epitaph aptly describes the unusual and colorful life of this man, one of the great evangelical preachers of the eighteenth century. His testimony was, “By the grace of God, I am what I am!”

“Amazing Grace” was a hymn published in 1779, with words written in 1772 by the English poet and Anglican clergyman John Newton (1725–1807). “Amazing Grace” is probably the most beloved hymn of the last two centuries. This hymn is estimated to be performed 10 million times annually. It has appeared on over 11,000 albums and translated into about 60 languages. It was referenced in Harriet Beecher Stowe’s anti-slavery novel Uncle Tom’s Cabin. It had a surge in popularity during two of America’s greatest crises: the Civil War and the Vietnam War.

Ironically, this stirring song, closely associated with the African-American community, was written by a former slave trader, John Newton.

John was born on July 24, 1725, in Wapping, England, to a seafaring father, John Newton, Sr., and a devout Christian mother, Elizabeth Newton. His father loved him but was gone at sea most of the time. On the other hand, his mother was tender and nurturing, teaching him the Word of God. She would instruct him in memorizing the Bible whole chapters at a time and took him to church. Unfortunately, when he was almost seven, his mother died of tuberculosis. His father remarried a short time later and sent him to a boarding school. During his time at the boarding school, he made bad friends. His character disintegrated to the point that he was dismissed from one school and moved to another. By the time he was 11 years old, the boarding schools didn’t want him, so his father took him along to sea. He spent the next six years on the Atlantic Ocean with his father.

When John was 17, his father arranged to send him to Jamaica for a well-paying job overseeing a plantation. On his way, while waiting for the ship’s departure, John received an invitation to the home of some old-time friends, the Catletts. It was in this home that John’s mother had died ten years earlier. As he reacquainted himself with them, he got to know their daughter, Mary. John and Mary’s mothers were best of friends. John had been invited to stay four days, but he stayed two weeks and missed the ship to Jamaica.

At age 18, John was conscripted into the Royal Navy, and his life went from bad to worse. He wanted to return and see Mary, so he deserted the ship but was caught, publicly flogged, and laid in irons. His life on the ship was so profane that even the other ungodly sailors cringed at his curses and blasphemies. He gained the title “The Great Blasphemer” and was such an unwanted man on the ship that he was sent to work on a slave ship.

One of the owners of the slave ship where he now worked, offered John a job once they reached the African coast. However, once on shore, he was tied up and forced to work with little food, clothing, or shelter. He sent several letters back to his father during this time, pleading for help.

A ship called The Greyhound was sailing near the coast, which John had now called home. The captain had been instructed by John’s father to look for his son. The ship, while being almost too far from shore to trade, decided to give trading a try. A friend of John’s rowed out from shore to trade. As he turned to leave, the captain asked him whether he knew anyone named John Newton. He did to the captain’s surprise, and John was brought on board to go home.

On board the ship, Newton picked up a copy of Thomas á Kempis’s Christian classic, The Imitation of Christ. He had never encountered anything like it, and he began to wonder if the Christian claims might be true. That night, on March 10, 1748, a fierce storm nearly swamped the ship. Men, animals, and provisions were swept overboard. The storm awakened Newton, the ship’s rotten timbers broken by the waves and floodwater swirling into his cabin. John prayed for the first time in years.

The Greyhound thrashed about in the North Atlantic storm for over 11 days. With little hope of survival, the sailors mechanically worked the pumps, trying to keep the vessel afloat. On the eleventh day of the storm, John was too exhausted to pump, so he was tied to the helm, where he did his best to hold the ship to its course. From one o’clock until midnight, he was at the helm. He feared he was going to die, and if the Christian faith were true, then he surely would not be forgiven. He reflected on all he had done over the past few years. His life seemed as ruined and wrecked as the battered ship he was trying to steer through the storm. During those long and grueling hours, Newton cried out to God like he never had before, and that was the turning point in his life.

That was a day John Newton remembered ever after. “On that day, the Lord sent from on high and delivered me out of deep waters.” Over 50 years later, John wrote in his diary on March 21, 1805: “Not well able to write; but I endeavor to observe the return of this day with humiliation, prayer, and praise.”

Only God’s amazing grace could take a rude, profane, slave-trading sailor and transform him into a child of God. John never ceased to stand in awe of God’s work in his life. He took an interest in prayer, reading and meditating on the Scriptures, and only speaking words pleasing to God.

On his return home, Mary and her parents recognized the change the Lord had brought in John. The two were married on February 1, 1750.

For the next four years, Newton was captain of his own slave ship. This occupation kept him separated from Mary for months at a time. While they were apart, the two corresponded constantly. In his letters, John repeatedly wrote how their love and marriage increased his thankfulness and gratefulness to the Lord. “... When I indulge myself with a particular thought of you, it usually carries me on farther and brings me upon my knees to bless the Lord for giving me such a treasure and to pray for your peace and welfare”

John endeavored to “Christianize” his slave ship by holding Sunday services for his crew of 30 sin-hardened men. He made three more voyages to bring slaves from Africa to North America. As he planned his fourth trip, he became sick with malaria. God used this sickness to end his involvement in the slave trade.

As John began a new chapter in his life, he felt called to be a minister. For more than 50 years, he preached the gospel and was one of the most influential men of his day.

John Newton often composed a hymn to go with his Sunday evening services. In 1779, 280 of these were collected and combined with 68 hymns by Newton’s friend and parishioner, William Cowper, and published as the Olney Hymns. The most famous of all the Olney Hymns, “Faith’s Review and Expectation”, grew out of David’s exclamation in 1 Chronicles 17:16-17. We know it today as “Amazing Grace”. “Amazing Grace” originally had six stanzas, and the last verse was added about a century later. Most hymnals have four or five of these verses.

As minister in the church, John continued to be more and more troubled by the slave trade that was still going on. In 1788, 34 years after he left the slave trade, He wrote a book entitled Thoughts Upon the African Slave Trade and sent it to all the members of parliament. This book brought an awareness to the public of the evils of the slave trade. He quotes this, “Needless to say, the capturing, selling and transporting of black slaves to the plantations in the West Indies and America was a cruel and vicious way of life.” With the help and providence of God, John saw the day, several months before his death, in 1807, when slavery was officially banned from England.

When John was in his sixties, his beloved wife Mary passed away. This was a great trial for John, and he spent the remaining 17 years of his life without her.

After John suffered a stroke and shortly before his death, a spokesman for the church encouraged Newton to consider retiring from preaching because of failing health, eyesight, and memory. John replied, “What, shall the old African blasphemer stop while he can still speak? I will continue to preach. Although my memory’s fading, I remember two things very clearly: I am a great sinner, and Christ is a great Savior.”

The last words of John Newton as he lay on his deathbed were as follows: “I am still in the land of the dying; I shall be in the land of the living soon.”

The tune “Amazing Grace” is an early American folk melody. It was first known as a plantation melody entitled “Loving Lambs”. This tune was first published in 1831 in the book The Virginia Harmony. The majority of hymn books published after this time included this song. In 1910, Edwin O. Excell added the last verse, which eventually replaced the last three original verses of the song. His edition of the song is most common in our hymnals today. Several other Olney hymns by Newton continue to be sung today, including “How Sweet the Name of Jesus Sounds” and “Glorious Things of Thee are Spoken”.

Betapa tidak masuk akalnya bahwa Tuhan dapat mengambil seorang pendosa yang hina, tanpa takut akan Tuhan, dan menjadikannya seorang orang kudus yang telah dibasuh dengan darah serta pengkhotbah Injil! Dalam kisah ini, kita melihat kuasa mengubah hidup Allah bekerja dalam kehidupan penulis himne kita.

Di pemakaman kecil di halaman gereja di Olney, Inggris, berdiri sebuah batu nisan granit dengan tulisan ini, yang ditulis oleh Newton sendiri sebelum kematiannya:

John Newton, dahulu seorang tidak percaya dan hidup sembarangan, seorang pelayan budak di Afrika, oleh rahmat kaya dari Tuhan dan Juruselamat kita Yesus Kristus, dilindungi, dipulihkan, diampuni, dan ditetapkan untuk berkhotbah tentang iman yang dahulu lama ia usahakan untuk hancurkan!

Epitaaf ini tepat menggambarkan kehidupan luar biasa dan berwarna dari pria ini, salah satu pengkhotbah evangelis besar pada abad kedelapan belas. Kesaksiannya adalah, “Oleh anugerah Allah, aku adalah apa aku!”

“Amazing Grace” adalah sebuah himne yang diterbitkan pada 1779, dengan kata-kata yang ditulis pada 1772 oleh penyair Inggris dan rohaniwan Anglikan John Newton (1725–1807). “Amazing Grace” mungkin merupakan himne paling dicintai dalam dua abad terakhir. Diperkirakan himne ini diperdengarkan 10 juta kali setiap tahun. Ia muncul pada lebih dari 11.000 album dan diterjemahkan ke dalam sekitar 60 bahasa. Ia dirujuk dalam novel anti-perbudakan karya Harriet Beecher Stowe, Uncle Tom’s Cabin. Popularitasnya melonjak dua kali selama dua krisis terbesar Amerika: Perang Saudara dan Perang Vietnam.

Ironisnya, lagu yang menggugah ini, erat dikaitkan dengan komunitas Afrika-Amerika, ditulis oleh mantan pedagang budak, John Newton.

John lahir pada 24 Juli 1725, di Wapping, Inggris, dari seorang ayah pelaut, John Newton, Sr., dan seorang ibu Kristen yang saleh, Elizabeth Newton. Ayahnya menyayanginya tetapi sering berada di laut. Sebaliknya, ibunya lembut dan menyayangi, mengajarkan Firman Tuhan kepadanya. Ia mengajarinya menghafal kitab-kitab Alkitab per bab sekaligus dan membawanya ke gereja. Sayangnya, ketika ia hampir berumur tujuh tahun, ibunya meninggal karena tuberkulosis. Ayahnya menikah lagi tak lama kemudian dan mengirimnya ke sekolah asrama. Selama di sekolah asrama, ia berteman dengan teman-teman yang buruk. Karakternya memburuk sampai-sampai ia dikeluarkan dari satu sekolah dan dipindahkan ke sekolah lain. Pada usia sebelas tahun, sekolah-sekolah asrama tidak lagi menginginkannya, sehingga ayahnya membawanya ke laut. Ia menghabiskan enam tahun berikutnya di Samudra Atlantik bersama ayahnya.

Pada usia 17 tahun, ayahnya mengatur agar ia dikirim ke Jamaika untuk pekerjaan bergaji tinggi mengawasi sebuah perkebunan. Dalam perjalanan, saat menunggu keberangkatan kapal, John menerima undangan ke rumah beberapa teman lama, keluarga Catlett. Di rumah inilah ibu John meninggal sepuluh tahun sebelumnya. Saat ia kembali berkenalan dengan mereka, ia menjadi akrab dengan putri mereka, Mary. Ibu John dan ibu Mary adalah sahabat karib. John sedianya diundang untuk tinggal empat hari, tetapi ia tinggal dua minggu dan ketinggalan kapal ke Jamaika.

Pada umur 18 tahun, John direkrut paksa ke Angkatan Laut Kerajaan, dan hidupnya semakin memburuk. Ia ingin kembali menemui Mary, sehingga ia membelot dari kapal tetapi tertangkap, dicambuk di muka umum, dan dibelenggu. Kehidupannya di kapal begitu kotor sehingga bahkan pelaut-pelaut fasik lainnya merasa ngeri terhadap sumpah serapah dan hujatannya. Ia mendapat julukan “Pengejahat Besar” dan menjadi orang yang sangat tidak diinginkan di kapal sehingga ia dikirim bekerja di kapal budak.

Salah satu pemilik kapal budak tempat ia bekerja menawarinya pekerjaan begitu mereka mencapai pantai Afrika. Namun, setelah di darat, ia diikat dan dipaksa bekerja dengan sedikit makanan, pakaian, atau perlindungan. Ia mengirim beberapa surat kepada ayahnya selama masa ini, memohon pertolongan.

Sebuah kapal bernama The Greyhound sedang berlayar dekat pantai, yang kini John sebut rumah. Kapten kapal telah diperintahkan oleh ayah John untuk mencari putranya. Kapal itu, meskipun hampir terlalu jauh dari pantai untuk berdagang, memutuskan mencoba berdagang. Seorang teman John mendayung dari pantai untuk berdagang. Saat ia berbalik hendak pergi, sang kapten bertanya apakah ia mengenal seseorang bernama John Newton. Ia mengenalnya, mengejutkan sang kapten, dan John dibawa ke kapal untuk pulang.

Di atas kapal, Newton mengambil sebuah salinan karya klasik Kristen Thomas á Kempis, The Imitation of Christ. Ia belum pernah menemukan sesuatu seperti itu, dan ia mulai bertanya-tanya apakah klaim-klaim Kristen mungkin benar. Malam itu, pada 10 Maret 1748, sebuah badai hebat hampir menenggelamkan kapal. Manusia, hewan, dan bekal tersapu ke laut. Badai membangunkan Newton, kayu-kayu kapal yang lapuk dihantam ombak dan air banjir berputar-putar ke dalam kabinnya. John berdoa untuk pertama kalinya dalam bertahun-tahun.

The Greyhound bergelut dalam badai Atlantik Utara selama lebih dari 11 hari. Dengan sedikit harapan untuk selamat, para pelaut secara mekanis menggerakkan pompa, berusaha menjaga agar kapal tetap terapung. Pada hari kesebelas badai, John terlalu kelelahan untuk memompa, sehingga ia diikat pada kemudi, di mana ia berusaha sekuat tenaga mengarahkan kapal pada haluannya. Dari jam satu sampai tengah malam, ia berada di kemudi. Ia takut akan mati, dan jika iman Kristen itu benar, maka ia yakin tidak akan diampuni. Ia merenungkan semua yang telah dilakukannya selama beberapa tahun terakhir. Hidupnya tampak hancur dan remuk seperti kapal yang rusak yang ia usahakan kemudikan melintasi badai. Selama jam-jam panjang dan melelahkan itu, Newton berseru kepada Allah sebagaimana belum pernah dilakukannya sebelumnya, dan itu menjadi titik balik dalam hidupnya.

Itu adalah hari yang selalu diingat John sesudahnya. “Pada hari itu, Tuhan mengutus dari atas dan menyelamatkanku dari air yang dalam.” Lebih dari 50 tahun kemudian, John menulis dalam hariannya pada 21 Maret 1805: “Tidak terlalu mampu menulis; tetapi aku berusaha memperingati kembalinya hari ini dengan rendah hati, doa, dan pujian.”

Hanya anugerah Allah yang menakjubkan yang dapat mengambil seorang pelaut kasar, kotor, pedagang budak dan mengubahnya menjadi anak Allah. John tidak pernah berhenti takjub akan karya Allah dalam hidupnya. Ia menaruh minat pada doa, membaca dan merenungkan Kitab Suci, dan hanya berbicara kata-kata yang menyenangkan bagi Allah.

Setibanya di rumah, Mary dan orangtuanya mengenali perubahan yang dibawa Tuhan dalam diri John. Keduanya menikah pada 1 Februari 1750.

Selama empat tahun berikutnya, Newton menjadi kapten kapal budaknya sendiri. Pekerjaan ini membuatnya terpisah dari Mary berbulan-bulan lamanya. Saat mereka berjauhan, kedua orang ini terus-menerus berkorespondensi. Dalam surat-suratnya, John berulang kali menulis bagaimana kasih dan pernikahan mereka meningkatkan rasa syukur dan terima kasihnya kepada Tuhan. “... Ketika aku membiarkan diriku memikirkan engkau secara khusus, itu biasanya membawaku semakin jauh dan membuatku berlutut untuk memberkati Tuhan karena telah memberi padaku harta seperti itu dan untuk berdoa bagi damai dan kesejahteraanmu”

John berusaha “meng-Kristen-kan” kapalnya dengan mengadakan kebaktian hari Minggu bagi awaknya yang berjumlah 30 orang, keras dalam dosa. Ia melakukan tiga pelayaran lagi untuk membawa budak dari Afrika ke Amerika Utara. Saat merencanakan pelayaran keempatnya, ia jatuh sakit malaria. Tuhan memakai penyakit ini untuk mengakhiri keterlibatannya dalam perdagangan budak.

Saat John memulai babak baru dalam hidupnya, ia merasa dipanggil untuk menjadi seorang pengkhotbah. Selama lebih dari 50 tahun, ia berkhotbah Injil dan menjadi salah satu orang paling berpengaruh di zamannya.

John Newton sering menyusun sebuah himne untuk menyertai kebaktian malam Minggu. Pada 1779, 280 dari himne-himne ini dikumpulkan dan digabungkan dengan 68 himne oleh teman dan jemaat Newton, William Cowper, dan diterbitkan sebagai Olney Hymns. Yang paling terkenal dari semua Olney Hymns, “Faith’s Review and Expectation”, tumbuh dari seruan Daud dalam 1 Chronicles 17:16-17. Kita kenal sekarang sebagai “Amazing Grace”. “Amazing Grace” pada awalnya memiliki enam bait, dan bait terakhir ditambahkan sekitar satu abad kemudian. Sebagian besar buku himne memiliki empat atau lima bait dari himne ini.

Sebagai imam di gereja, John tetap semakin gelisah oleh perdagangan budak yang masih berlangsung. Pada 1788, 34 tahun setelah ia meninggalkan perdagangan budak, ia menulis sebuah buku berjudul Thoughts Upon the African Slave Trade dan mengirimkannya kepada semua anggota parlemen. Buku ini membangkitkan kesadaran publik akan kejahatan perdagangan budak. Ia menulis ini, “Tidak perlu dikatakan, penangkapan, penjualan dan pengangkutan budak kulit hitam ke perkebunan di Hindia Barat dan Amerika adalah cara hidup yang kejam dan jahat.” Dengan pertolongan dan pemeliharaan Allah, John menyaksikan hari itu, beberapa bulan sebelum kematiannya, pada 1807, ketika perbudakan secara resmi dilarang di Inggris.

Ketika John berusia enam puluhan, istri tercintanya Mary meninggal. Ini merupakan cobaan besar baginya, dan ia menghabiskan 17 tahun sisa hidupnya tanpanya.

Setelah John menderita stroke dan sesaat sebelum kematiannya, seorang juru bicara gereja menganjurkan Newton mempertimbangkan untuk pensiun dari berkhotbah karena kesehatan, penglihatan, dan ingatannya yang menurun. John menjawab, “Apa, apakah sang penghujat Afrika tua ini berhenti sementara ia masih dapat berbicara? Aku akan terus berkhotbah. Meskipun ingatanku memudar, aku ingat dua hal dengan sangat jelas: aku adalah seorang besar pendosa, dan Kristus adalah Juruselamat yang besar.”

Kata-kata terakhir John Newton saat berbaring di ranjang kematiannya adalah sebagai berikut: “Aku masih di tanah orang-orang yang sedang mati; Aku akan segera berada di tanah orang-orang yang hidup.”

Melodi “Amazing Grace” adalah melodi rakyat Amerika awal. Ia pertama kali dikenal sebagai melodi perkebunan berjudul “Loving Lambs”. Melodi ini pertama kali diterbitkan pada 1831 dalam buku The Virginia Harmony. Mayoritas buku himne yang diterbitkan setelah waktu ini memasukkan lagu ini. Pada 1910, Edwin O. Excell menambahkan bait terakhir, yang akhirnya menggantikan tiga bait asli terakhir dari lagu tersebut. Edisinya dari lagu ini paling umum dalam buku himne kita hari ini. Beberapa Olney hymns lain karya Newton terus dinyanyikan hingga sekarang, termasuk “How Sweet the Name of Jesus Sounds” dan “Glorious Things of Thee are Spoken”.
